mcqs.question: In Amdahl's Law formula, speedup = 1 / ((1-p) + p/s), what happens to the (1-p) term as more processors are added?
options: It shrinks proportionally with processor count
It stays exactly the same, since it represents work that can't be sped up at all
It grows, because more processors add coordination overhead to the serial term
It disappears entirely once s exceeds 2
mcqs.explanation: (1-p) represents the strictly serial portion of the work, which by definition doesn't benefit from more processors — it's a fixed cost regardless of s. It doesn't shrink, doesn't grow with processor count in the basic formula, and never vanishes at any value of s.

mcqs.question: A program is 50% parallelizable (p=0.5) and gets an ideal 4x speedup (s=4) on that portion. What is the overall speedup?
mcqs.explanation: speedup = 1 / ((1-0.5) + 0.5/4) = 1 / (0.5 + 0.125) = 1 / 0.625 = 1.6x. The large serial half caps the achievable speedup well below the 4x applied to the parallel portion alone.

mcqs.question: A program has a serial fraction of 25% (p=0.75 parallelizable). What is the maximum possible speedup, even with infinite processors?
options: Unbounded — infinite processors mean unbounded speedup
mcqs.explanation: As s approaches infinity, speedup approaches 1/(1-p) = 1/0.25 = 4x — a hard ceiling regardless of processor count. Speedup is never unbounded when any serial fraction exists at all, however small.

mcqs.question: Why does using a static count of "parallelizable instructions" as p often overestimate real-world speedup?
options: Because instruction counts are always measured incorrectly by profilers
Because it omits synchronization, communication, and coordination overhead introduced by parallelizing, which behaves as additional serial-equivalent cost
Because Amdahl's Law only applies to single-threaded programs
Because compilers always parallelize more instructions than a static count predicts
mcqs.explanation: Real parallel execution introduces overhead — locks, barriers, data movement between processors — that a static instruction count never sees, and that overhead behaves exactly like serial time in Amdahl's formula. It's not a profiler-measurement error, and the law is specifically about parallel vs serial execution, so it doesn't only apply to single-threaded code.
